name: Spring rate
seoDesc: Spring rate: work out external diameter from the shear modulus and the wire diameter. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Spring rate calculator turns the shear modulus, the wire diameter and more into external diameter. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Spring rate calculator work?
sections.html:
The Spring rate calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports external diameter in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the spring ends); then you type in the shear modulus (G), the wire diameter, the active coils and the spring rate.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in pascals. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as closed and squared/ground, double closed and open. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A number, expressed in coils.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in newtons per meter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 12 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Spring rate calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

External diameter=wire diameter + (1 ÷ 2) × (shear modulus (G) × (wire diameter ^ 4) ÷ (active coils × spring rate))
Internal diameter=external diameter − 2 × wire diameter
Total coils=active coils + spring ends

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Shear modulus (G) = 10 Pa, Wire diameter = 30 mm, Spring ends set to Open and Active coils = 10. Working through the relationship above gives External diameter = 76.6085 mm, Internal diameter = 16.6085 mm and Total coils = 10.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: External diameter = 76.6085 mm, Internal diameter = 16.6085 mm and Total coils = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Shear modulus (G) = 10 Pa and Wire diameter = 30 mm.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Force per length, opening in newtons per meter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Spring rate calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the shear modulus, the wire diameter and the active coils — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Spring rate calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns external diameter, derived from the shear modulus, the wire diameter and the active coils. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Spring rate calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the shear modulus, the wire diameter, the active coils and the spring rate, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter shear modulus (G) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Shear modulus (G) opens in pascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports External diameter = 76.6085 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Spring rate calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
